sections.heading: What you get
paragraphs: Mimosa hostilis root bark, milled to a fine, even powder. It is the same bark as our [shredded](/product/shredded-mimosa-hostilis-root-bark) and [whole](/product/whole-mimosa-hostilis-root-bark) cuts, taken all the way down to a powder, and in the bag it reads mauve to red-brown depending on the light.

The plant is Mimosa tenuiflora, still sold under its older name Mimosa hostilis, a thorny tree of the legume family native to northeastern Brazil and southern Mexico. In Brazil it is called jurema preta. The root bark is the part dyers want: it is dense with tannins and with the red-purple pigments that make it one of the few natural dyes that goes straight from bag to pot without a separate mordant for most wool work.

sections.heading: Why choose the powder over shredded bark?
paragraphs: Speed and concentration. A powder has far more surface in contact with the water than a strand of bark, so it gives up its color in a fraction of the simmer time. That makes it the cut for small, controlled jobs: test skeins, dye samples, a single scarf, and soap, where you want color in the oil rather than a pot to strain. [Why particle size changes everything in a dye pot](/blog/why-particle-size-changes-everything-in-a-dye-pot) goes into the trade-off in detail.

The price of that speed is straining. Powder stays suspended, so a powder bath has to be settled and poured off or run through fine cloth before the fiber goes in, or specks will lodge in the wool. If you are dyeing a full fleece or several pounds of yarn, the [shredded cut](/product/shredded-mimosa-hostilis-root-bark) is easier to lift out and gives more than one bath. [The three cuts of Mimosa root bark, and who each one suits](/blog/the-three-cuts-of-mimosa-root-bark) compares all three side by side.

sections.heading: What colors does Mimosa hostilis powder give?
paragraphs: On wool and silk, a first bath gives dusky pinks, plum and a warm red-brown; more bark and a longer simmer push it toward burgundy and a deep chocolate. A little alum in the fiber first brightens the pinks. An iron afterbath turns the same bath slate, charcoal or near-black, which is one of the reasons dyers keep a pound of this on the shelf: one material, two very different palettes. [Iron as a modifier, and how far to go](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go) shows how quickly that shift happens.

The pot's pH moves the color as well. Keep the bath neutral to slightly acidic if you want to stay in the purples, and expect browns if it drifts alkaline. [Keeping a bark bath purple instead of brown](/blog/keeping-a-bark-bath-purple) is the short version of how to hold it there.

Cotton and linen take the color more palely than wool and silk, because plant fibers have no protein for the tannins to bind to. Mordanting them with tannin and then alum first closes most of that gap; [wool, silk, cotton and linen in the same bath](/blog/wool-silk-cotton-and-linen-in-the-same-bath) shows the difference on one set of swatches.

sections.heading: How much powder do you need per pound of fiber?
paragraphs: Dyers measure bark against the dry weight of the fiber, written as a percentage "of weight of fiber" (WOF). A pale tint takes about 25 to 40 percent, 4 to 6 ounces for a pound of wool; a mid shade about 50 to 75 percent, 8 to 12 ounces; and the deepest plums up to an equal weight of bark and fiber. Powder gives up its color most completely, so start at the lower end of each range.

That makes a quarter pound enough to learn on with a few test skeins, and a full pound enough for one to two pounds of fiber in mid shades. [How much bark per pound of fibre](/blog/weighing-bark-against-fibre) has the full table, and [testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece) is worth ten minutes before the first big pot.

sections.heading: Using it in cold-process soap
paragraphs: Soap makers use the powder for color alone: it gives bars in tones from warm tan to dusky brown-purple depending on how much goes in and how it is added. The usual routes are infusing the powder in part of the recipe's oil and straining it, or adding a small amount at light trace. Start low, since the color deepens as the bar ages over the following weeks. [Bark as a colourant in cold process soap](/blog/bark-as-a-colourant-in-cold-process-soap) walks through both methods.
We make no claim about what the bark does for skin; it is sold here as a colorant.

faqs.question: Do I need a mordant with Mimosa hostilis?

paragraphs: Root bark of Sassafras albidum, cut into pieces: warm red-brown, with the spicy scent the tree is known for. Sassafras is a member of the laurel family native to eastern North America, from southern Maine to eastern Texas, and the easiest tree in an American wood to recognize by its three leaf shapes on one branch.

It is one of the older dye materials on the continent, and the root bark is the part that carries the most color. [Sassafras albidum, a North American dye tree](/blog/sassafras-albidum-the-north-american-dye-tree) tells more of that story.

sections.heading: What colors does sassafras root bark dye?

It pairs well with Mimosa hostilis: an overdye of sassafras on a pale [Mimosa hostilis](/product/shredded-mimosa-hostilis-root-bark) pink pushes it toward coral and terracotta.

A reasonable starting amount is 25 to 50 percent of the dry fiber's weight, since sassafras is lighter in color than Mimosa bark. As with any new dye, test a small skein first; see [testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece).
Beyond the dye pot, the dried bark is used for its scent in potpourri blends and in historical and educational craft displays.

faqs.answer: On wool it gives warm tans, orange-browns and rose-browns. Alum mordant makes the color clearer and brighter, and an iron afterbath shifts it to soft greys and grey-browns. Wool and silk take it best.

faqs.question: Is sassafras root bark legal to buy?
faqs.answer: Yes, as raw botanical material for dyeing and craft. Federal rules prohibit safrole, oil of sassafras and sassafras bark intended for flavoring from use in human food (21 CFR 189.180), so it is sold here for dyeing and craft only and not for human consumption.

faqs.question: How much sassafras root bark do I need to dye wool?
faqs.answer: Start around 25 to 50 percent of the dry fiber weight, which is 4 to 8 ounces for a pound of wool. Sassafras is lighter in color than Mimosa bark, so it takes more for the same depth.

faqs.question: Can sassafras be combined with Mimosa hostilis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Overdyeing sassafras on a pale Mimosa hostilis pink moves it toward coral and terracotta, and the two share a dye pot well on alum-mordanted wool.

faqs.question: How is the root bark packed?
faqs.answer: In a double-sealed, smell-proof bag that is flushed with nitrogen before sealing. Nitrogen displaces the oxygen inside the bag, which stops the bark oxidizing, so the color and freshness hold in transit and in storage. Reseal the bag after each use to keep it that way.

faqs.question: Where does it ship from?
faqs.answer: From California, to US addresses only, with tracking once payment is confirmed. Parcel orders from 100 dollars ship free.
